That's why zero_result_rate is best used as a production monitoring signal, watched over time for trend changes and spot-checked case by case, rather than as a single offline pass/fail gate. A sudden jump after a deploy is a fast early warning that needs no ground truth and is worth investigating immediately; it complements the periodic, deeper golden-dataset evaluation.

exercises.prompt: An evaluation reports hit rate: the share of questions whose expected document appears in the top 3 results. The search function below is meant to be evaluated as-is, but the score is suspiciously perfect because the evaluation leaks the answer. Find and fix the bug.
exercises.code:
index = {
    "refunds": "Refunds take 5 business days.",
    "password": "Reset your password from the login page.",
    "billing": "Update billing details in settings.",
}

def search(query, k=3, expected=None):
    words = set(query.lower().split())
    ranked = sorted(index, key=lambda d: -len(words & set(index[d].lower().split())))
    if expected is not None and expected not in ranked[:k]:
        ranked.insert(0, expected)
    return ranked[:k]

golden = [("how long do refunds take", "refunds"), ("I cannot sign in", "password")]
hits = sum(1 for q, doc in golden if doc in search(q, k=1, expected=doc))
print(hits / len(golden))   # should reflect real search quality, not always 1.0
hints: What does the search function do with the expected answer?
Could the search ever miss when it is told the answer?
Evaluation must call the retriever exactly as production does, without the label.
exercises.solutionCode:
index = {
    "refunds": "Refunds take 5 business days.",
    "password": "Reset your password from the login page.",
    "billing": "Update billing details in settings.",
}

def search(query, k=3):
    words = set(query.lower().split())
    ranked = sorted(index, key=lambda d: -len(words & set(index[d].lower().split())))
    return ranked[:k]

golden = [("how long do refunds take", "refunds"), ("I cannot sign in", "password")]
hits = sum(1 for q, doc in golden if doc in search(q, k=1))
print(hits / len(golden))   # 0.5: 'I cannot sign in' misses with k=1
exercises.solutionExplanation: The search function accepted the expected document and inserted it into the results whenever it was missing, so every evaluation question was a hit and the score was always 1.0. That is label leakage: the system under test saw the answer. Removing the parameter and calling search exactly as production does reveals the real hit rate, here 0.5 at k=1, because the keyword ranking puts the wrong document first for 'I cannot sign in': the billing document wins on the shared word 'in', and the password document shares no words with the query. Keep evaluation code separate from retrieval code and never pass labels into the component being measured.

assessments.prompt: A developer manually tries several queries against a retrieval system and concludes it's working well because every result they see looks relevant. Why does this kind of manual check systematically tend to miss false negatives (relevant documents that should have been retrieved but weren't)?
options: Manual checks are just as good at catching false negatives as automated evaluation, as long as the developer is careful.
Manual checks miss false negatives only when the reviewer is unfamiliar with the underlying corpus.
False negatives only occur when the embedding model is outdated, which a manual check can always detect by inspecting the model's version number.

A human reviewing a list of returned results can only judge what's actually visible in front of them; a relevant document that should have appeared but didn't is, by definition, not present in that list, so there's nothing in the reviewer's field of view to prompt them to notice its absence.
assessments.explanation: A false negative's defining characteristic is that it's a document that should be in the results but isn't -- there's no representation of 'the thing that's missing' anywhere in what a reviewer is actually looking at, so nothing prompts them to go looking for it. This is a structural limitation of reviewing visible output, independent of how careful or diligent the reviewer is, which is why the “Manual checks are just as good…” option is wrong: more care doesn't create visibility into something that isn't there. The “False negatives only occur when the embedding…” option invents an unrelated, narrow cause (model staleness) as if it were the general explanation. The “Manual checks miss false negatives only…” option is also wrong: even a reviewer deeply familiar with the corpus faces the same structural blind spot, since familiarity with the corpus doesn't make an absent result visible in the list being reviewed.

assessments.prompt: A developer tests their retrieval system with queries phrased using the same vocabulary the underlying documents use, and it scores excellently. Real user queries, phrased more casually with different words, score much worse against that exact same, unchanged retriever. What does this illustrate?
options: This proves the retriever is fundamentally unusable and should be discarded entirely in favor of a completely different architecture.
Query selection bias: developers reuse vocabulary from the documents, which isn't how real users phrase queries.
This is expected and not actually a concern, since developer-style queries are the primary use case any real system needs to support well.
The retriever must have been silently reconfigured between the two tests, since one unchanged system cannot legitimately produce two different scores.
assessments.explanation: This is the query selection bias the explanation describes: the same, unchanged retriever produces very different scores purely because of which queries were used to test it, since a developer's own vocabulary tends to overlap heavily with the documents' vocabulary in a way real users' paraphrased, casual phrasing does not. The “The retriever must have been silently reconfigured…” option wrongly assumes the retriever itself must have changed, when the worked example holds it fixed and only varies the query set. The “This proves the retriever is fundamentally unusable…” option draws an overly drastic conclusion from a specific, well-understood, and addressable bias, rather than a wholesale architectural failure. The “This is expected and not actually…” option inverts the lesson: real user phrasing, not developer phrasing, is what the system actually needs to handle well in production.

assessments.prompt: After an index parameter change, a developer manually re-checks only the two queries they happened to test during initial development, both of which still return correct results, and concludes the change is safe. What does this kind of manual spot-check fail to protect against?
options: It fails only in the specific case where the developer forgets to round their reported recall numbers to three decimal places.
It fails to protect only against changes to the embedding model specifically; index parameter changes are inherently always safe to validate through manual spot-checking alone.
It fails to protect against regressions in query patterns the developer didn't happen to re-check.
Nothing -- if the two originally-tested queries still return correct results, this is mathematically sufficient to guarantee that no other query pattern has regressed.
assessments.explanation: This is the structural limitation the explanation describes: manual spot-checking doesn't run again automatically and only covers whatever specific queries someone happened to re-try, so a regression affecting different query patterns produces no signal at all to a reviewer who never looked at those patterns: that is the gap an automated check against the full golden dataset closes by re-running every case every time. The “It fails to protect only against changes…” option invents an unfounded exemption for one category of change. The “Nothing -- if the two originally-tested queries…” option overclaims a guarantee that two correct results provide no actual basis for. The “It fails only in the specific case…” option trivializes a structural blind spot into a cosmetic rounding issue, which isn't the mechanism at play.

assessments.prompt: Why is a metric like zero-result rate (the fraction of real queries that come back with no results after filtering) valuable as a production monitoring signal, distinct from offline golden-dataset evaluation?
options: It requires no relevance labels or human judgment at all and can be tracked continuously on live traffic, catching problems in close to real time that a periodically-run, fixed offline golden dataset hasn't yet been extended to cover.
It is a complete replacement for golden-dataset evaluation, since it directly measures whether the results a query does return are actually relevant.

It can only be computed by re-running a system against the fixed historical queries already present in the golden dataset, not against real, live production traffic, so it can only confirm problems that offline evaluation has already found and reported.
It only becomes a meaningful signal once the underlying golden dataset has grown to include at least several hundred queries.
assessments.explanation: The explanation frames zero-result rate as valuable because it needs no relevance labels: it's a measurable signal computed continuously on live traffic, catching a category of problem (queries returning nothing) as it happens, well before a periodic golden-dataset run would surface it, and independent of which cases the golden dataset already covers. The “It is a complete replacement for golden-dataset…” option overclaims: the explanation presents it as one layer among several (alongside golden-dataset evaluation and periodic manual review), not a replacement for judging actual relevance. The “It only becomes a meaningful signal once…” option invents a dependency on golden-dataset size that doesn't exist; zero-result rate is computed directly from a live query log, unrelated to the golden dataset's size. The “It can only be computed by re-running…” option reverses the relationship: zero-result rate is valuable BECAUSE it runs against real production traffic, not fixed historical queries.

assessments.prompt: A teammate says the RAG chatbot 'must be retrieving fine' because its answers read fluently and confidently. Explain why that reasoning is unreliable and what you'd check instead.
assessments.modelAnswer: Fluency and confidence are properties of the language model's writing, not evidence about the quality of the context it was given. An LLM has no built-in way to detect that its retrieved context is irrelevant or wrong, and a capable model will write an equally well-written, equally confident response whether or not the chunks support the answer. This is the RAG hallucination failure mode covered earlier in this subject: a confidently wrong answer and a confidently correct one can look identical from the outside. Judging retrieval quality by reading the chatbot's answers checks the wrong layer of the pipeline, two steps removed from the thing that needs validating. Instead, I'd check the retrieved context directly: pull the raw chunks handed to the model for several real queries (ideally randomly sampled, not hand-picked) and verify whether they contain the information needed to answer correctly, independent of how the model phrased its response. Beyond that spot check, I'd want the layered approach from this concept: an automated evaluation of retrieval (not final answers) against an independently labeled golden dataset that reruns on every relevant change, plus production signals like zero-result rate that don't depend on reading any generated text. Confident-sounding output is, at best, a signal about the language model, not a substitute for checking what retrieval handed it.
